title: Direct & Inverse Proportion
prerequisites: Comfort with ratios and percentages from Chapter 8.
Basic idea of variables and simple equation solving from Chapter 2.
Understanding of multiplication and division of fractions.

topics.title: Direct Proportion
topics.quick_summary: Two quantities are in direct proportion when they increase or decrease together at the same constant rate, so their ratio always stays the same.

detailed.definition: Two quantities x and y are in direct proportion if y = kx for some constant k (called the constant of proportionality), meaning x/y stays constant as both quantities change together.
detailed.key_idea: In direct proportion, if one quantity is multiplied or divided by a certain factor, the other quantity changes by the EXACT SAME factor in the SAME direction (both increase together, or both decrease together).
detailed.working_principle: If x1/y1 = x2/y2 (the ratio stays constant), the quantities are in direct proportion; this relationship is used to set up and solve for an unknown value using cross-multiplication: x1y2 = x2y1.
applications: Scaling recipes up or down while keeping ingredient ratios the same.
Currency conversion, fuel consumption vs. distance travelled, and speed-distance calculations at constant speed.

topics.real_life: The cost of fruit increases directly with the quantity bought — if 2 kg of apples costs ₹200, then 4 kg costs ₹400, always keeping the same cost-per-kg ratio.
points: Direct proportion rule: x/y = k (constant) for all corresponding pairs of values.
As x increases, y increases in the same ratio; as x decreases, y decreases in the same ratio.
To solve, set up x1/y1 = x2/y2 and cross-multiply to find the unknown quantity.
A direct proportion graph (y vs x) is always a straight line passing through the origin.
mistakes: Confusing direct proportion with a general linear relationship — a direct proportion graph must pass through the ORIGIN (0,0).
Setting up the ratio upside down (x1/y1 = y2/x2) when cross-multiplying.
Applying direct proportion logic to situations that are actually inversely proportional (e.g., speed and time for a fixed distance).
topics.memory_hook: 'Both go up together, or both go down together' — the ratio between them never changes.
topics.advanced: The constant of proportionality k in y = kx has real physical meaning in many contexts — for cost vs. quantity, k is simply the price per unit; for distance vs. time at constant speed, k is the speed itself — recognising k's real-world meaning makes proportion problems far more intuitive than pure algebra.

topics.title: Inverse Proportion
topics.quick_summary: Two quantities are in inverse proportion when one increases as the other decreases such that their PRODUCT always stays constant.

detailed.definition: Two quantities x and y are in inverse proportion if xy = k for some constant k, meaning as x increases, y decreases proportionally so their product remains fixed.
detailed.key_idea: In inverse proportion, if one quantity is multiplied by a certain factor, the other quantity is divided by that SAME factor — they move in OPPOSITE directions, unlike direct proportion where they move together.
detailed.working_principle: If x1y1 = x2y2 (the product stays constant), the quantities are in inverse proportion; this relationship is used to solve for an unknown using x1y1 = x2y2 directly.
applications: Work-and-time problems (more workers/machines finish a fixed job faster).
Speed and time for a fixed distance (faster speed means less time taken).

topics.real_life: The number of workers needed and the time taken to finish a fixed job are inversely proportional — more workers means the job finishes in less time, but workers × time (total work) stays the same.
points: Inverse proportion rule: x × y = k (constant) for all corresponding pairs of values.
As x increases, y decreases in exactly the same ratio, and vice versa (opposite directions).
To solve, set up x1y1 = x2y2 and solve for the unknown quantity directly.
An inverse proportion graph (y vs x) is a smooth curve (hyperbola shape), never a straight line.
mistakes: Setting up a direct-proportion-style ratio (x1/y1 = x2/y2) for a problem that is actually inversely proportional.
Forgetting that inverse proportion means multiplying one quantity requires DIVIDING the other by the same factor, not multiplying both.
Assuming a graph of an inverse relationship is a straight line — it is always a curve.
topics.memory_hook: 'One goes up, the other comes down — product stays locked' — xy = k is the signature of inverse proportion.
topics.advanced: Recognising WHICH type of proportion applies in a word problem is often the hardest step — a useful test is to ask: 'if I double one quantity, does the other double too (direct), or does it halve (inverse)?' — this quick mental check prevents most proportion-type mix-ups before any calculation begins.

formulas.name: Inverse Proportion Relation
formulas.variables: x1, y1 = first pair of corresponding values; x2, y2 = second pair; both pairs share the same constant product k.
formulas.when_to_use: Whenever two quantities are confirmed to be inversely proportional (their product stays fixed).
formulas.common_mistakes: Confusing this with the direct-proportion cross-multiplication rule x1y2 = x2y1.
formulas.shortcut: Remember: inverse proportion PAIRS multiply straight across (x1y1 = x2y2), unlike direct proportion which cross-multiplies.
